channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: First human model for form of inherited heart disease uses realistic levels of mutant protein
item.description: Inherited cardiomyopathies—diseases of the heart muscle, which cause the heart to have a harder time pumping blood to the rest of the body—are the leading cause of heart failure in young adults. Desmin-related cardiomyopathy (DRM) is one such familial disease that affects approximately 1 in 2,000 individuals worldwide. No disease-specific therapies exist for DRM, with patients receiving only generic heart failure medicines.

item.title: Shopping for a 2027 health plan? State aid and 4 smart moves can cut your health costs
item.description: Residents of at least 11 states who buy coverage through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace can get extra state help paying their premiums in 2027.

item.title: New guidance outlines use of first immunotherapy for children newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes
item.description: For the first time, children ages 8 to 17 who are newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have access to an approved treatment that targets the underlying autoimmune disease, rather than solely managing blood sugar levels with insulin.

item.title: Rare genetic discovery explains sex development differences in two XY sisters
item.description: Two young girls in Vietnam are living proof that there is a lot more to sex than genetics, after being found to have an extremely rare sexual development condition.

item.title: First complete genomes for neglected malaria parasites revealed
item.description: Scientists have produced gold-standard reference genomes for previously neglected malaria parasites by sequencing low-input DNA directly from patient blood, bypassing lab culture.

item.title: AI used to better predict kidney stone composition
item.description: Mayo Clinic researchers developed and tested an artificial intelligence (AI) model that used results from a standard 24-hour urine test to predict kidney stone composition more accurately than a conventional urine-based calculation. Using the AI model, researchers correctly predicted kidney stone composition in 73% of patients, compared with 33% using the conventional calculation alone.

item.title: Cell changes around early breast cancers provide clues to why some cases become invasive
item.description: Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have created one of the most detailed maps to date of the cell environment surrounding ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), the most common form of preinvasive, or stage 0, breast cancer. The findings may help explain why some lesions progress to invasive breast cancer and others do not, informing strategies to improve patient risk prediction and develop better targeted approaches for patients at higher risk of invasive disease.

item.title: American Cancer Society updates prostate cancer screening guideline: Regular PSA testing for average- and high-risk men
item.description: The American Cancer Society (ACS) today released an updated guideline for prostate cancer screening to help find cancer before it spreads and reduce the risk of dying from the disease. Key changes include a direct recommendation for prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening every two years for average-risk men aged 50–69, with clinicians ensuring patients understand the potential benefits, limitations and harms before starting screening. Also, ACS recommends annual PSA-based screening beginning at 45 years old for Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer.

item.title: Inflammation is involved in the earliest stages of atherosclerosis
item.description: Inflammation plays an important role in the development of atherosclerosis from its earliest stages, long before the onset of symptoms or cardiovascular events such as heart attack or stroke. This is the main conclusion of a study led by a team at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC) and published in the European Heart Journal. The research shows that systemic inflammation contributes to disease development independently of traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as elevated cholesterol and hypertension.

item.title: Trump administration will fund new research on controversial psychedelic drug ibogaine
item.description: Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.

item.title: New guidelines recommend regular prostate cancer screening for all middle-aged men
item.description: Experts now recommend regular prostate cancer screening for all men ages 50 to 69 and earlier for higher-risk groups, according to new American Cancer Society (ACS) guidelines.

item.title: Surveyed cancer patients say cannabis improves symptoms
item.description: A new study by the University of Kentucky Markey Cancer Center and the Kentucky Cannabis Center provides insight into how some cancer patients are using cannabis, the benefits they report and how physicians can help patients make informed decisions.

item.title: Mice help researchers discover how the COVID virus triggers sneezing and coughing
item.description: In the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, as Diana Bautista and others in her UC Berkeley lab suffered sneezing and coughing fits and achy bodies, she asked an interesting scientific question: How, exactly, do viruses cause the noxious symptoms we're all familiar with from bouts with colds, the flu and COVID?

item.title: Smelling Parkinson's: From discovery to skin swab test
item.description: A retired nurse who noticed that people with Parkinson's had a distinct odor inspired Manchester scientists to explore changes in molecules on the skin's surface. Using a simple skin swab, they can detect about 15,000 molecular features, approximately 10% of which consistently differ in abundance between people with and without Parkinson's.

item.title: Combination therapy overcomes treatment resistance in breast cancer models
item.description: A combination approach successfully overcame treatment resistance and led to durable responses in preclinical models of advanced breast cancer, according to researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center. The targets at the center of this approach were identified by a new computational biology algorithm developed at UT MD Anderson called TargetScore, suggesting this tool could be used to develop new therapeutic strategies and advance precision oncology.

item.title: Grief's physical symptoms are real. Here's what you can do to help
item.description: Grief can ravage your mind, but science shows it can also weaken your body, leaving you more vulnerable to illness.

item.title: Scientists identify protein driving age-related organ damage
item.description: Monash University researchers have identified a protein that drives age-related damage in vital organs, opening a potential new avenue for treatments that could help people stay healthier as they get older. Published in Immunity, the research revealed a link between the protein granzyme K and signs of aging in the heart, liver and kidneys.

item.title: College student mental health improves, but significant needs remain
item.description: College students are reporting lower rates of depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts, continuing a multiyear pattern of improvement, according to recent findings from the 2025–2026 Healthy Minds Study.

item.title: Blood thinner could offer a new way to treat osteoarthritis
item.description: Osteoarthritis is the most common form of joint disease, a condition that causes joints to become painful and stiff. It can happen to any joint when the cartilage cushioning the ends of bones breaks down or wears away. Currently, there are no approved drugs to slow or stop the underlying disease. But there is a promising development from an unexpected quarter—a blood thinner.

item.title: Three decision-making styles emerge when people weigh probability words against numbers, researchers report
item.description: We don't all understand the same words in the same way, and this can affect the choices we make, according to researchers including those from the University of Tokyo. A team sought to compare how people with an autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and people without ASD interpret probability terms. They found that people with and without ASD could be divided into three groups of decision-makers, whose judgment varied depending on the relative influence of positive or negative framing and the numerical probabilities they inferred from verbal expressions. This work highlights the importance of dialogue to check whether people have understood information as intended and to support informed decision-making.

item.title: Moderna's RSV vaccine shown to provide strong protection against serious cases in adults 50 and older
item.description: A single dose of Moderna's mResvia RSV vaccine was 60.3% protective against documented respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections, 60.2% against RSV-associated emergency department or urgent care encounters and 81.8% against RSV-associated hospitalizations in a population of older U.S. veterans, according to a recent study in JAMA Network Open.

item.title: Study explores leveraging dental hygienists to expand access to oral health care
item.description: Dental hygienists play a critical role in delivering preventive oral health care, helping patients maintain good oral health and preventing more serious and costly dental problems. Yet in many states, laws and regulations governing the dental hygiene profession can limit where and how hygienists practice—potentially restricting patients' access to essential preventive services.

item.title: Five lifespan-extending treatments boost the same antioxidant in mice
item.description: Aging is about far more than wrinkles and gray hair, despite what social media and advertisements might have us believe. The real concern lies beneath the surface, where the biology of aging is intertwined with a host of diseases, from heart disease to neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's to metabolic disorders and cancer. Targeting the processes that make the body age could have effects far beyond any single disease, potentially easing the burden of several age-related conditions at once.

item.title: New atlas traces how key human brain cells develop before and after birth
item.description: Scientists have long known that many developing brain cells originate in one region and migrate to another as they mature. But tracing the molecular changes that occur along that journey has been difficult, in part because some of the temporary prenatal brain structures that give rise to these cells largely disappear around birth.

item.title: Mapping the marmoset's deep-brain cell diversity and building a tool to integrate data across species
item.description: Researchers have built a high-resolution brain-cell atlas that could do for neuroscience what the Human Genome Project did for genetics. By charting over 25 million individual brain cells across humans, macaques and marmosets, a team of neuroscientists, computational biologists and software engineers across 55 institutions, including Princeton, produced a cellular roadmap of the basal ganglia, a deep-seated network of brain regions that aid movement, habit formation and decision-making.

item.title: Researchers pioneer new technology to track brain tissue from laboratory to data
item.description: Scientists studying the human brain have long faced a complex obstacle: because of the scarcity of neurotypical human brain tissue, tissue samples from a single brain must be shared across research entities. Those entities then generate massive amounts of data from their research but often lack a coordinated way to share, combine or reuse the information.

item.title: Researchers play critical role in developing new atlas of brain cells
item.description: Capturing a complete picture of what causes brain diseases from schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease to addiction has long been a challenge for scientists. But a growing body of evidence indicates that all seem related to the basal ganglia—a group of structures found in the center of the brain that control the body's movements, decision-making processes and habit formation.

item.title: High-fat diet may increase colon cancer risk by changing intestinal stem cells
item.description: Researchers at Arizona State University, U.S., have found that a high-fat diet leaves lasting changes in intestinal stem cells, potentially increasing the risk of tumor development.

item.title: Human basal ganglia atlas reveals how genes are regulated in individual cells
item.description: Salk Institute researchers have contributed to a landmark accomplishment in neuroscience: a 3D atlas of the human basal ganglia with single-cell genetic and epigenetic detail, published as a collection of 28 papers across Cell Press journals. The basal ganglia are a group of nerve cells that sit deep in the brain, where they control key functions like learning, emoting and moving. Basal ganglia dysfunction can lead to conditions like Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Tourette syndrome and addiction.

item.title: Cheap drug may prevent second stroke by lowering blood pressure
item.description: It's vital to lower blood pressure after a stroke, so the survivor doesn't suffer another as they recover. And it appears this safety measure can be achieved on the cheap, a new study says.
